content: There's a lot of text in Tau Ceti's README, but despite reading all that, I'm still confused on what's the difference between the various projects other than "we have lower code quality bar than Mathlib"

Maybe a diagram like this in the README (just a sketch at the moment) could be useful (if I understood correctly the difference between the projects?) Plus some common/uncommon pitfalls.

flowchart TD
    A[Start] --> B{What's the
        code quality?}
    B -->|Beautiful and fully general| C[Cool, probably mathlib]
    B -->|Barely tolerable| D{What is the content?}
    D -->|Reusable textbook formalization| H["Tau Ceti
        (make sure it is
        in the roadmap first)"]
    D -->|One-off or frontier
        research paper| K[Lean Pool]
    B -->|Unacceptable| G{Does it
        have `sorry`?}

        code has value?}

        with the domain-specific
        expertise?}

        Turing machines?}
    E -->|no| D

        The actual code can
        be discussed later.]
    R -->|no| R2[Sorry, we don't trust your
        code to be good.
        As of September 2026,
        LLM-generated code
        is terrible.
        ]
    H --> H2{Will it get
        into Mathlib
        eventually?}
    H2 -->|I'll clean up

(paste into e.g. mermaid.live to see the diagram graphically)

This flow chart is pretty good!

I would be slightly more positive about the quality of the the code the LLMs produce in September 2026, but no real argument about how that quality relates to what Mathlib and Tau Ceti want.

Re: the box the separates Tau Ceti and Lean Pool, I think I wouldn't use the word "textbook" necessarily, but it is a good approximation. Tau Ceti is for material that we believe will be reused. Essentially, if it's in a textbook, probably yes, if it is in a research paper and has already been built upon by >10 "downstream" research papers, then probably yes as well. If it's in a research paper that doesn't already have a bunch of citations, probably not.

Would you be interested in clarifying that in the flowchart slightly, and maybe trying to make it look slightly nicely / readable at reasonable settings? I'd like to include it!

Slightly updated version. Changes:

  • I add a "Yes" branch to "Does it have 'sorry'" block pointing to merely-true. Somehow I forget it last time.
  • I add a "Do you know the math in it?" conditional block. I think the "Yes" branch is correct, but the other branches may need modifications.
  • Fixed the textbook conditional as suggested above.
  • About LLM code quality: if reader overestimates it, the project gets low-quality contribution, which is bad. If reader underestimates it, they might scrutinize the code more carefully, which is likely good. Only downside I can think of is if some rogue AI becomes sentient and destroys everyone who makes fun of them, but that's obviously impossible :upside_down:
  • Not sure if there should be a dropout branch from Tau Ceti/Lean Pool to merely-true. It seems like there should be, but my current understanding is everything that can fit in merely-true can also fit in Lean Pool with some tokens and zero human effort.

I'm acutely aware that one needs zooming and panning to read the diagram, but mermaid seems not that configurable. I'll figure out something (or ask LLM to do so, we'll see).

Maybe change "is it sorry-free" to "is it sorry-and-axiom-free"?
Maybe for the "yes" branch of "does your code have value" say "improve the code to change your answers and try again"?

I would say the operational distinction between tau ceti and lean pool is:

  • do you already have a complete formalization? LeanPool
  • do you want to formalize something specific? Tau Ceti (new roadmap) or Lean Pool
  • do you just want to contribute tokens? Tau Ceti
